title: Byzantine and Christian Egypt
subtitle: 300–641 AD · The End of the Temples, the Coptic Church, and the Coming of Islam

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Egypt in the Christian Roman empire — the Augustal prefect, the patriarchs of Alexandria as a rival power, and the Persian and Arab conquests

entries.label: Constantine and the Christian turn
entries.hint: Under Constantine, Christianity went from persecuted to favoured. The toleration of 313 was followed by imperial patronage of the church; Constantine summoned the Council of Nicaea in 325 to settle the Arian dispute that began in Alexandria; and from 330 the grain that had fed Rome for three centuries was redirected to feed his new capital, Constantinople. The province was reordered again, and its bishop of Alexandria began to matter to emperors.
entries.note: Eusebius, Life of Constantine, Historia Ecclesiastica 10. The grain to Constantinople: the Theodosian Code and Justinian's Edict 13. Roger Bagnall, Egypt in Late Antiquity (1993) pp.1–20, 285–89.

entries.label: The Augustal Prefecture and the diocese of Egypt
entries.hint: Diocletian's and Constantine's reforms broke Egypt into a set of small provinces — Aegyptus, Augustamnica, Arcadia, the Thebaid, the Libyas — grouped as a diocese under the praefectus Augustalis at Alexandria, with civil government separated from military command and a dux for frontier defence. Justinian's edict of 539 partly reversed this, recombining civil and military power in each province's governor to make the machine work. The apparatus stayed recognisably Roman down to the Arab conquest.
entries.note: Justinian, Edict 13 (539). The provincial structure: Bernhard Palme, 'The Imperial Presence: Government and Army', in R.S. Bagnall (ed.), Egypt in the Byzantine World (2007); J.G. Keenan and the papyri of the office.

entries.label: Julian and the pagan last stand
entries.hint: The emperor Julian tried to roll the empire back to the old gods, reopening temples and restoring sacrifice. In Alexandria the news let a mob seize and lynch the deeply unpopular Arian bishop George of Cappadocia and two officials, burning the bodies and scattering the ashes 'so no shrine could be raised'. Julian merely reprimanded the city. His death on campaign in Persia two years later ended the reaction; no emperor after him favoured paganism.
entries.note: Ammianus Marcellinus 22.11; Socrates, Historia Ecclesiastica 3.2–3; Julian, Letter 21 (to the Alexandrians). Christopher Haas, Alexandria in Late Antiquity (1997) pp.280–95.

entries.label: Theodosius I outlaws the old gods
entries.hint: Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the empire's only lawful religion and, in a series of edicts culminating in 391–392, banned all sacrifice and closed the temples. In Alexandria that same year the patriarch Theophilus led the demolition of the Serapeum. When Theodosius died in 395 the empire was permanently divided, and Egypt, with its grain and its turbulent church, belonged to the eastern half ruled from Constantinople.
entries.note: Theodosian Code 16.10.10–12. The Serapeum: Rufinus, Historia Ecclesiastica 11.22–30; Socrates 5.16–17. Garth Fowden, 'Bishops and Temples in the Eastern Roman Empire', JTS 29 (1978).

entries.label: Marcian, Chalcedon and the killing of Proterius
entries.hint: The emperor Marcian convened the Council of Chalcedon in 451, whose definition of Christ 'in two natures' Egypt overwhelmingly rejected. When the imperial candidate Proterius was installed as patriarch of Alexandria under military guard, the city seethed; on Marcian's death in 457 a mob seized Proterius in the baptistery, killed him, dragged the body through the streets and burned it. From then on the imperial and the Egyptian churches were at war.
entries.note: Evagrius, Historia Ecclesiastica 2.5, 2.8; Zachariah of Mytilene 3.11–4.1. W.H.C. Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972) pp.148–83.

entries.label: Justinian and Egypt
entries.hint: Justinian's wars of reconquest ran on Egyptian grain and taxes. He reorganised the province's government by the edict of 539, closed the temple of Isis at Philae around 537 — the last functioning temple of the old Egyptian religion — and sent missionaries who converted the Nubian kingdom of Nobadia. His wife Theodora shielded the persecuted Miaphysite leaders, and the plague of 541, which reached the empire through the Egyptian port of Pelusium, killed a large share of the population.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 1.19 (Philae), Secret History; John of Ephesus. Justinian's Edict 13. Plague: Procopius, Wars 2.22–23; Peter Sarris, 'The Justinianic Plague', Continuity and Change 17 (2002).

entries.label: Heraclius — Egypt lost and lost again
entries.hint: Heraclius rose to power on a revolt launched from Roman Africa and Egypt against the tyrant Phocas. He then lost Egypt to Persia for a decade (619–629), recovered it by treaty, and tried to reunite the fractured church with a compromise formula, Monotheletism, enforced in Egypt by the patriarch and governor Cyrus 'the Caucasian' with a persecution the Coptic sources call the worst they had known. It left Egypt bitterly divided and militarily hollow when the Arab armies arrived at the end of his reign.
entries.note: Nicephorus, Short History; the Chronicle of John of Nikiou. Walter Kaegi, Heraclius: Emperor of Byzantium (2003) and Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992).

entries.label: Athanasius — bishop against the world
entries.hint: Athanasius held the see of Alexandria for 45 turbulent years, defending the Nicene doctrine that the Son is fully God against the Arian party favoured by a run of emperors. He was deposed and exiled five times, twice fleeing to the desert monks whose cause he championed and whose founder he memorialised in the Life of Antony. He built the patriarchate into a power that emperors had to reckon with and bound it permanently to the monastic movement.
entries.note: Athanasius, Orations against the Arians, Life of Antony, Festal Letters, Apology to Constantius. Timothy Barnes, Athanasius and Constantius (1993); David Brakke, Athanasius and the Politics of Asceticism (1995).

entries.label: Theophilus — the temple-breaker
entries.hint: Theophilus turned the patriarchate into a machine of Christianisation and church politics. He led the destruction of the Serapeum in 391 and the conversion of pagan sites into churches, then reversed his own theology to purge the Origenist monks of Nitria (the 'Tall Brothers'), whose flight to Constantinople helped bring down John Chrysostom. Ruthless and effective, he handed a dominant see to his nephew and pupil Cyril.
entries.note: Socrates, Historia Ecclesiastica 6.7; Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom. Norman Russell, Theophilus of Alexandria (2007).

entries.label: Cyril of Alexandria — the arbiter of orthodoxy
entries.hint: Cyril, Theophilus's nephew, was the age's most formidable theologian of the Incarnation — his formula for the unity of Christ shaped every later council — and its most aggressive churchman. Early in his tenure he expelled the Jewish community of Alexandria and clashed with the prefect Orestes in the poisoned atmosphere that led to Hypatia's murder in 415. In 431 he dominated the Council of Ephesus, had his rival Nestorius condemned in absentia, and made Alexandria the judge of what counted as orthodox.
entries.note: Cyril, On the Unity of Christ, Twelve Anathemas, Letters. Socrates 7.7, 7.13–15. Susan Wessel, Cyril of Alexandria and the Nestorian Controversy (2004); John McGuckin, St Cyril of Alexandria (1994).

entries.label: Dioscorus and the Chalcedonian rupture
entries.hint: Cyril's successor Dioscorus pushed Alexandrian dominance too far: at a council at Ephesus in 449, backed by imperial troops and monks, he rehabilitated the extreme Eutyches and had his opponents beaten — a session the pope called a 'robbery'. Two years later the Council of Chalcedon reversed it, defined Christ 'in two natures', and deposed and exiled Dioscorus. The Egyptian church refused to accept either his deposition or the definition, and the split became permanent.
entries.note: Acts of the Council of Chalcedon (Richard Price & Michael Gaddis translation, 2005). W.H.C. Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972) pp.1–49.

entries.label: The two patriarchs of Alexandria
entries.hint: After Chalcedon, Alexandria usually had two rival patriarchs: an anti-Chalcedonian (Miaphysite) one recognised by the great majority of Egyptian Christians, and a Chalcedonian one — nicknamed 'Melkite', the king's man — installed and protected by the imperial garrison, often unable to move freely in his own city. The theologian Severus of Antioch took refuge in the Egyptian desert; Coptic and Melkite churches, calendars and monasteries ran in parallel for nearly two centuries.
entries.note: Zachariah of Mytilene; the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria. Ewa Wipszycka, The Alexandrian Church: People and Institutions (2015); Frend (1972) pp.143–295.

entries.label: Benjamin I — the Coptic Church survives the conquest
entries.hint: Benjamin I became Coptic patriarch just before the Persians came, fled the Byzantine Monothelete persecution under Cyrus, and spent thirteen years in hiding among the monasteries of the Thebaid. After the Arab conquest the general 'Amr ibn al-'As, told the true head of the Egyptian church was in exile, sent him a safe-conduct; Benjamin returned to Alexandria in 644, recovered the churches the Melkites had held, and re-established the Coptic hierarchy that has continued unbroken since.
entries.note: History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria (the 'Life of Benjamin' by his contemporary); John of Nikiou, ch.120–21. C. Detlef G. Müller, and Phil Booth, 'The Last Years of Cyrus, Patriarch of Alexandria', Travaux et Mémoires 20/1 (2016).

entries.label: The Persian occupation of Egypt
entries.hint: In 619 the army of Khosrow II under the general Shahrbaraz overran Egypt, taking Alexandria after a siege, and ended seven centuries of unbroken Roman rule. For a decade Egypt was a Sasanian province, its administration continuing in Greek and Coptic under Persian oversight, its grain no longer sailing to Constantinople — a loss that helped push the eastern empire to the brink. Heraclius's victories over Persia forced the army's withdrawal by treaty in 629.
entries.note: The Persian-period papyri (Greek, Coptic and a few Middle Persian): Bernhard Palme and others. Chronicle of John of Nikiou. James Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010).

entries.label: The Arab conquest of Egypt
entries.hint: 'Amr ibn al-'As entered Egypt from Palestine in December 639 with a few thousand men, took Pelusium, beat the Byzantine field army at Heliopolis in July 640, and after a seven-month siege forced the surrender of the great fortress of Babylon in April 641. Alexandria, defended but demoralised and led by the compromised governor-patriarch Cyrus, was handed over by treaty; the last Byzantine troops sailed in September 642. A naval attempt to retake the city in 645 failed.
entries.note: Chronicle of John of Nikiou (ch.111–21); al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr. Alfred J. Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1902; 2nd ed. 1978); Hugh Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007) pp.144–68.

entries.label: 'Amr ibn al-'As and the founding of Fustat
entries.hint: 'Amr governed the new province from a garrison town, Fustat, laid out around his army's camp beside the fortress of Babylon — the settlement that would grow into Cairo — where he built the first mosque in Africa. The bulk of the population kept its Coptic church and paid a land-and-poll tax (kharaj and jizya); the Greek-speaking Byzantine elite largely left. Egyptian grain was again shipped east, now to Medina, along a re-dug Red Sea canal.
entries.note: Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr. The bilingual Greek–Arabic papyri of the conquest generation (PERF 558, the earliest dated Arabic document, 643). Petra Sijpesteijn, Shaping a Muslim State (2013); Wladimir Kubiak, Al-Fustat: Its Foundation and Early Urban Development (1987).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Christian street wars of Alexandria, the desert raids of the Blemmyes and Nobades, the Persian occupation, and the Arab conquest

entries.label: The destruction of the Serapeum
entries.hint: After Theodosius's edicts banned the temple cults, a confrontation in Alexandria escalated into a siege of the Serapeum by pagans who had seized Christian hostages. When an imperial rescript pardoned the pagans but ordered the temple destroyed, the patriarch Theophilus led a crowd that tore down the colossal statue of Serapis and demolished the sanctuary and its library. Nothing else so clearly marked the end of the old religion in its greatest stronghold.
entries.note: Rufinus, Historia Ecclesiastica 11.22–30; Sozomen 7.15; Eunapius, Lives of the Sophists (a hostile pagan account). Johannes Hahn, Gewalt und religiöser Konflikt (2004).

entries.label: The murder of Hypatia
entries.hint: Hypatia, head of the Neoplatonist school of Alexandria and a respected mathematician and astronomer, was a friend and adviser of the imperial prefect Orestes, then locked in a power struggle with the patriarch Cyril. A rumour that she was the obstacle to their reconciliation led a mob, including church attendants called parabalani, to drag her from her carriage into a church, kill her, and burn the body. The killing shocked contemporaries and has stood ever since as the symbol of faith turned murderous.
entries.note: Socrates, Historia Ecclesiastica 7.15; the Suda; John of Nikiou 84 (a hostile version). Maria Dzielska, Hypatia of Alexandria (1995); Edward Watts, Hypatia (2017).

entries.label: The street wars of Christian Alexandria
entries.hint: For over a century, control of the see of Alexandria was fought in the streets. Disputed elections brought riots; bishops installed by emperors were besieged in their churches or lynched (George in 361, Proterius in 457); rival congregations, the church strongmen known as parabalani, and imperial troops all played a part. The city's habit of settling religious questions by force — inherited from its Greek–Jewish–pagan quarrels — made it ungovernable on any other terms.
entries.note: Athanasius, History of the Arians; Socrates and Sozomen, passim. Christopher Haas, Alexandria in Late Antiquity (1997); Ewa Wipszycka on the parabalani.

entries.label: The raids of the Blemmyes and Nobades
entries.hint: With Rome's frontier pulled back to Aswan, the desert peoples the sources call Blemmyes and Nobades raided Upper Egypt and the Western oases, plundering monasteries and towns and reaching Philae, where the Blemmyes still worshipped Isis and periodically borrowed her statue. A treaty negotiated by the general Maximinus in 452 bought a hundred-year peace, and over the following century missionaries drew both peoples into Christianity.
entries.note: Priscus of Panium, fragments; Procopius, Wars 1.19. László Török, Between Two Worlds (2009) pp.515–26; the Blemmyan documents from Gebelein.

entries.label: Enforcing Chalcedon by force
entries.hint: For 85 years the empire tried to make Egypt accept the Council of Chalcedon, and Egypt would not. The imperial patriarch Proterius was murdered by the crowd in 457; anti-Chalcedonian patriarchs were exiled again and again; troops were sent against Alexandrian congregations; a formula of compromise, the Henotikon of 482, satisfied no one; and Justinian finally deposed the last non-Chalcedonian patriarch, Theodosius, in 536. The result was not conformity but a settled, self-conscious separate Egyptian church.
entries.note: Evagrius, Historia Ecclesiastica 2–4; Zachariah of Mytilene. Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972); Volker Menze, Justinian and the Making of the Syrian Orthodox Church (2008).

entries.label: Egypt and the fall of Phocas
entries.hint: When the exarch of Africa raised a revolt against the emperor Phocas, he sent his nephew Nicetas to take Egypt while his son Heraclius sailed for Constantinople. Nicetas defeated Phocas's general Bonosus in hard fighting around Alexandria and secured the province — and with it the grain supply and a treasury — for the rebellion that made Heraclius emperor. It showed again that whoever held Egypt could make an emperor.
entries.note: Chronicle of John of Nikiou 107–10; Nicephorus, Short History 1–2. Walter Kaegi, Heraclius (2003) pp.37–48.

entries.label: The Persian conquest of Egypt
entries.hint: The Sasanian general Shahrbaraz, having taken Syria and Palestine, invaded Egypt in 617–618 and captured Alexandria in 619 after a siege — reportedly betrayed through an unguarded canal culvert. It was the first time in nearly 950 years, since Alexander, that Egypt had passed out of Greek or Roman hands, and for the eastern empire the loss of its grain and revenue was close to fatal.
entries.note: Chronicle of John of Nikiou 109–10; the Khuzistan Chronicle; the Life of Anastasius the Persian. Clive Foss, 'The Persians in the Roman Near East', JRAS 13 (2003).

entries.label: Heliopolis and the siege of Babylon
entries.hint: 'Amr ibn al-'As, reinforced to perhaps 15,000 men, defeated the Byzantine field army under Theodore at Heliopolis in July 640, scattering the garrison of the Delta. He then laid siege to the fortress of Babylon at the head of the Delta, the key to Egypt; after seven months and the failure of relief, and with the governor Cyrus negotiating behind the walls, it surrendered on 9 April 641. The road to Alexandria lay open.
entries.note: John of Nikiou 111–17; al-Baladhuri; Ibn Abd al-Hakam. Alfred Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1902) pp.234–320; Hugh Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007).

entries.label: The fall of Alexandria
entries.hint: The patriarch-governor Cyrus, sent back from exile to make terms, signed a treaty with 'Amr on 8 November 641: an eleven-month truce, payment of tribute, and the peaceful evacuation of the Byzantine forces. Alexandria — walled, garrisoned and reachable by sea, and in no military sense beaten — was handed over on 17 September 642. A Byzantine fleet retook it briefly in 645; 'Amr recovered it, and Roman rule in Egypt was finished for good.
entries.note: The 'Treaty of Alexandria': John of Nikiou 120; al-Tabari. Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1902) pp.320–68; Phil Booth, 'The Muslim Conquest of Egypt Reconsidered', Travaux et Mémoires 17 (2013).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The late-antique province, the great estate, the church as landlord and welfare state, and the rise of the local strongman

entries.label: The late-antique provincial state
entries.hint: The Roman machine kept running, reformed. Egypt was a diocese of small provinces under the Augustal prefect, with civil and military commands divided, sprawling bureaus (officia), and a tax system shifting from grain toward gold assessed on a fixed multi-year cycle. But the curial class that had run the towns was collapsing under the fiscal burden, and its functions drifted toward bishops, great landowners and appointed strongmen — the state present everywhere on paper, thin on the ground.
entries.note: Roger Bagnall, Egypt in Late Antiquity (1993) pp.54–92, 153–71; Bernhard Palme in Bagnall (ed.), Egypt in the Byzantine World (2007). Tax in gold: A.H.M. Jones, The Later Roman Empire (1964).

entries.label: The great estate — the house of Apion
entries.hint: The archive of the Apion family, senators and consuls who owned vast estates around Oxyrhynchus, is the most detailed picture of a landholding operation to survive from antiquity: thousands of documents recording rents in kind and cash, granaries and wine presses, irrigation machinery, a payroll of tenants, guards and craftsmen, a private prison, and a private armed retinue. The house also collected the public taxes of its district and delivered them to the state — a fusion of private wealth and public function.
entries.note: The Oxyrhynchus Apion papyri: E.R. Hardy, The Large Estates of Byzantine Egypt (1931); Todd Hickey, Wine, Wealth, and the State in Late Antique Egypt: The House of Apion at Oxyrhynchus (2012); Peter Sarris, Economy and Society in the Age of Justinian (2006).

entries.label: The pagarch and the retreat of the salaried state
entries.hint: By the sixth century a district was often run by a pagarch — in practice a great local landowner given responsibility for its taxes and public order, holding an office that shaded into a private lordship. Villages complained bitterly of pagarchs who over-assessed, quartered troops, and jailed defaulters. The state increasingly governed the countryside not through its own officials but by delegating to whoever was already powerful there, a pattern that would carry straight through the Arab conquest.
entries.note: J.G. Keenan, 'The Aphrodite Papyri and Village Life in Byzantine Egypt', Bulletin de la Société d'Archéologie Copte 26 (1984); the petitions of Dioscorus of Aphrodito against the pagarch. Bagnall, Egypt in Late Antiquity (1993) pp.161–65.

entries.label: The church as an arm of government
entries.hint: The Christian church became a public institution. A bishop's court had legal standing; the church was, after the state and the great houses, the largest landowner in Egypt; and it ran the welfare the classical city never had — grain doles, hospitals, orphanages, the ransoming of captives, hostels for travellers. The bishop was often the effective 'father of the city', negotiating with governors, tax officials and, in the end, conquerors.
entries.note: Ewa Wipszycka, Les ressources et les activités économiques des églises en Égypte (1972) and The Alexandrian Church (2015). Peter Brown, Poverty and Leadership in the Later Roman Empire (2002).

entries.label: Roman codes and Coptic contracts
entries.hint: The formal law was the Theodosian Code of 438 and Justinian's Corpus of 534, administered in Greek by imperial judges. But in the villages a growing share of everyday business — sales, leases, loans, marriage settlements, wills, dispute settlements — was written in Coptic, with its own set formulae, before local scribes, priests or monastic notaries. A distinct provincial legal practice, part Roman and part Egyptian, ran under the imperial one and outlasted it.
entries.note: Coptic legal documents: Artur Steinwenter, Das Recht der koptischen Urkunden (1955); Leslie MacCoull, Coptic Legal Documents (2009). The Greek framework: Joseph Mélèze Modrzejewski.

entries.label: The village of Aphrodito and its notary
entries.hint: The Upper Egyptian village of Aphrodito held the rare privilege of paying its taxes directly to the state rather than through a pagarch, and fought to keep it. Its records survive largely through Dioscorus, a landowner, lawyer, notary and Greek poet who drafted the village's contracts and petitions and represented it at Constantinople. His archive is the fullest view anywhere of how an ordinary late-Roman village actually worked — its land, its church, its feuds, its dealings with the powerful.
entries.note: The Dioscorus archive: Jean-Luc Fournet (ed.), Les archives de Dioscore d'Aphrodité cent ans après leur découverte (2008); Leslie MacCoull, Dioscorus of Aphrodito: His Work and His World (1988).

entries.label: The frontier army and its collapse
entries.hint: Late Roman Egypt was held by a field army near Alexandria and a screen of frontier troops (limitanei) in fortified Nile towns, backed by federate arrangements paying the Nobades and Blemmyes to keep the peace. It was enough for raiders and internal disorder but had hollowed out by the seventh century: the Persians overran the country in two years, and 'Amr ibn al-'As conquered it with a force that at its largest numbered perhaps fifteen thousand men.
entries.note: The Notitia Dignitatum (Or. 28, 31). Bernhard Palme, 'The Imperial Presence', in Bagnall (ed.), Egypt in the Byzantine World (2007); Constantin Zuckerman, Du village à l'empire (2004) on the Thebaid garrison.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The end of the temples, the Arian and Christological wars, the Chalcedonian schism, and the desert fathers

entries.label: The end of the temples
entries.hint: Across the fourth to sixth centuries the temples of Egypt were closed, converted to churches, quarried, or simply left to the sand as their endowments were confiscated and their priesthoods dispersed. The last hieroglyphic inscription was cut at Philae in 394, the last text in Demotic there in 452, and around 537 Justinian's officers shut the Isis temple of Philae itself — the final working sanctuary of a religion three and a half thousand years old.
entries.note: Last hieroglyphic and Demotic graffiti at Philae: the 'Esmet-Akhom' inscription (394) and the 452 text. Procopius, Wars 1.19.36–37. Jitse Dijkstra, Philae and the End of Ancient Egyptian Religion (2008); David Frankfurter, Religion in Roman Egypt (1998).

entries.label: The Arian and Christological wars
entries.hint: Alexandria was where the empire's great doctrinal fights began. The priest Arius' teaching that the Son was a created being provoked the Council of Nicaea in 325, which defined him as 'of one being' with the Father — a formula Athanasius spent his life defending against Arian emperors. A century later the question shifted to how godhead and manhood met in Christ: Cyril of Alexandria's insistence on their unity, against Nestorius, carried the Council of Ephesus in 431 and made Alexandrian theology the standard of orthodoxy.
entries.note: Athanasius, Orations against the Arians. Acts of Nicaea and Ephesus. R.P.C. Hanson, The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God (1988); John McGuckin, St Cyril of Alexandria and the Christological Controversy (1994).

entries.label: Chalcedon and the birth of the Coptic Church
entries.hint: The Council of Chalcedon in 451 defined Christ as existing 'in two natures', divine and human. Egypt read this as a betrayal of Cyril and a concession to Nestorius, and held instead to 'one incarnate nature' of the Word — Miaphysitism. Despite eighty-five years of imperial pressure, the Egyptian church refused to conform, and became a distinct communion, increasingly identified with the Coptic language and a sense of Egyptian religious nationhood: the Coptic Orthodox Church, still separate today.
entries.note: Acts of Chalcedon (Price & Gaddis, 2005). W.H.C. Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972); Aziz Atiya, A History of Eastern Christianity (1968); Stephen Davis, The Early Coptic Papacy (2004).

entries.label: Antony and the birth of the desert life
entries.hint: Around 270 a young Egyptian named Antony gave away his land and withdrew, first to the edge of his village and then deep into the Eastern Desert, to seek God in solitude and struggle with demons. Athanasius' Life of Antony, written soon after his death, became one of the most widely read books of late antiquity and the template for the ascetic vocation. Thousands followed him into the deserts of Egypt — 'the desert was made a city', in a famous phrase.
entries.note: Athanasius, Life of Antony (Greek text; the earlier Coptic tradition). Samuel Rubenson, The Letters of St. Antony (1995); David Brakke, Demons and the Making of the Monk (2006).

entries.label: Pachomius and the invention of the monastery
entries.hint: Where Antony's followers lived alone, Pachomius gathered his in a walled community at Tabennesi around 320, with a written Rule governing common prayer, common meals, assigned work, dress and the day's hours, under an abbot. By his death he headed a federation of nine monasteries and two nunneries with thousands of members. This cenobitic model — the organised, rule-bound monastery — is Egypt's, and it became the standard form of monastic life across the entire Christian world.
entries.note: The Pachomian Koinonia (Armand Veilleux's translation, 1980–82): the Lives, the Rule, the letters. James Goehring, Ascetics, Society, and the Desert (1999); Philip Rousseau, Pachomius (1985).

entries.label: The monastic desert and its export
entries.hint: The monastic settlements of the Wadi Natrun and the Nile-Delta desert — Nitria, the 'Cells' of Kellia, Scetis — became the spiritual capital of Christendom. Their teaching survives as the Apophthegmata, the terse Sayings of the Desert Fathers; Evagrius Ponticus turned it into a system of the spiritual life; and a stream of visitors — Palladius, John Cassian, the authors of the Historia Monachorum — carried Egyptian monastic practice to Palestine, Constantinople, Gaul and eventually the Latin west.
entries.note: The Apophthegmata Patrum: Benedicta Ward's translation (1975). Historia Monachorum in Aegypto; Palladius, Lausiac History; John Cassian, Institutes and Conferences. Hugh Evelyn White, The Monasteries of the Wâdi 'n Natrûn (1926–33).

entries.label: Shenoute and the White Monastery
entries.hint: Shenoute of Atripe ruled the White Monastery near Sohag for some eight decades, a federation of several thousand monks and nuns held to a fierce discipline. He led armed raids on the temples and estates of the region's surviving pagan landowners, fed refugees from Blemmyan raids by the thousand, browbeat governors, and left an enormous body of sermons, rules and letters — the greatest achievement of literary Coptic and the model of the powerful Egyptian abbot.
entries.note: Shenoute's corpus: Stephen Emmel, Shenoute's Literary Corpus (2004); the ongoing editions. Ariel López, Shenoute of Atripe and the Uses of Poverty (2013); Rebecca Krawiec, Shenoute and the Women of the White Monastery (2002).

entries.label: The shrines of the saints and martyrs
entries.hint: Christian Egypt replaced the temple oracle with the saint's tomb. The greatest shrine was Abu Mina, west of Alexandria, built over the grave of the soldier-martyr Menas: a pilgrimage city with a basilica, baths and hostels, whose little terracotta flasks stamped with the saint between two camels have been dug up from Britain to the Sudan. The dead were healed by sleeping at such shrines, the martyrs' acts were the popular reading, and the calendar itself began from the 'Era of the Martyrs'.
entries.note: Abu Mina: Peter Grossmann, Abu Mina I: Die Gruftkirche und die Gruft (1989). Menas ampullae: Zsolt Kiss and others. Arietta Papaconstantinou, Le culte des saints en Égypte des Byzantins aux Abbassides (2001).
